paragraphs: A representation can capture useful hidden structure even when its reconstruction error looks worse. This paper constructs a mathematically tractable example of that mismatch, while explaining why nonlinear autoencoders can discover patterns that principal component analysis, or PCA, cannot detect.

The proposed high-dimensional model contains two latent factors. One affects covariance, the statistical structure that PCA uses. The other is statistically dependent yet uncorrelated, so its presence becomes visible only through higher-order moments. This distinction gives the researchers a controlled setting in which linear and nonlinear methods have different access to the underlying structure.

The authors prove that a minimal nonlinear autoencoder extracts both factors, whereas PCA and linear autoencoders fail to recover the second. They analyze both population risk and learning through empirical risk minimization. In this model, the nonlinear autoencoder can recover richer latent structure despite having higher reconstruction loss. The result shows why self-supervised test loss can be a misleading measure of representation quality, even in a setting that permits rigorous analysis.
icml-2026-a-solvable-high-dimensional-mo.tldr: A tractable model proves that nonlinear autoencoders can recover structure missed by PCA even while having worse reconstruction loss.

paragraphs: Preference-based language model training depends on judgments about which responses are better. Collecting these judgments can be expensive, particularly when relevant expertise or resources are scarce. ActiveUltraFeedback addresses that cost by choosing which responses should receive annotation as data collection proceeds.

The pipeline uses uncertainty estimates to identify informative annotation candidates dynamically. Its modular design allows systematic comparisons between standard selection methods and two proposed methods: Double Reverse Thompson Sampling and DeltaUCB. These new methods prioritize response pairs with large predicted quality differences, drawing on findings that such pairs can provide useful signals for fine-tuning.

In the reported experiments, datasets assembled through this pipeline improve downstream performance. Some results match or exceed those of static selection baselines using as little as one-sixth of the annotated data. This finding supports selective annotation as a way to make preference data collection more efficient: the usefulness of a dataset depends on which comparisons it contains, as well as how many judgments were collected.
icml-2026-activeultrafeedback-efficient-.tldr: ActiveUltraFeedback selects informative preference comparisons, achieving comparable or better downstream results with as little as one-sixth of the annotated data.

paragraphs: Physics-informed neural networks solve partial differential equations by incorporating differential relationships into learning. Making these networks deeper introduces a particular difficulty: derivatives with respect to the input can become numerically unstable. The paper distinguishes these vanishing or exploding differentials from the more familiar vanishing or exploding gradients associated with training.

The authors examine the computation graph used to calculate derivatives and identify bottlenecks that worsen with network depth. Their proposed architecture uses Coupling Layers whose Jacobian matrices have carefully controlled spectral norms. These controls regulate how differential information changes as it passes through layers, supporting more consistent propagation through a deep network.

The reported evaluations show that this approach improves stability and outperforms both conventional shallow physics-informed networks and alternative deep designs across challenging problems. The significance is architectural: increasing depth requires attention to the derivative calculations that the physical equations demand. By addressing those calculations directly, the method makes deeper networks more usable for the PDE-solving settings studied.
icml-2026-deep-coupling-learning-for-sol.tldr: Coupling Layers with controlled Jacobian spectral norms stabilize input derivatives and improve deep physics-informed neural networks for solving PDEs.

paragraphs: Sequential conformal prediction uses past prediction errors to quantify uncertainty in new predictions. Its validity depends on residual exchangeability, an assumption that temporal dependence and changing distributions can violate. Existing approaches try to compensate by reweighting observations, but choosing suitable weights remains difficult.

DistMatch instead recursively divides residuals into groups using a binary tree. Each split is guided by the Kolmogorov–Smirnov statistic, which compares distributions. The authors theoretically show that this procedure produces approximately exchangeable groups at the tree’s leaves. The approach therefore seeks useful local groupings without requiring a reweighting scheme.

Within each leaf, quantile regression receives online updates, allowing uncertainty estimates to adapt locally as new observations arrive. Experiments report better performance than existing sequential conformal prediction methods and improved robustness to distribution shifts. The central contribution is a way to organize historical errors into more suitable calibration groups. Its theoretical claim is approximate exchangeability within those groups, which preserves the qualification behind the method’s uncertainty reasoning.
icml-2026-distmatch-adaptive-binning-via.tldr: DistMatch groups prediction errors by distribution and updates local quantile models to improve sequential uncertainty estimation under distribution shifts.

paragraphs: Creating a useful visualization involves more than writing code for a chart. Professional work also includes repairing existing artifacts, adapting them to different data and tools, and clarifying what a user wants. DV-World evaluates visualization agents across these broader responsibilities through a benchmark containing 260 tasks.

The benchmark has three domains. DV-Sheet covers chart and dashboard creation in native spreadsheets, along with diagnostic repair. DV-Evolution tests adaptation of reference visualizations to new data across programming paradigms. DV-Interact introduces ambiguous requirements and a user simulator, testing whether an agent proactively works toward a clearer understanding of the intended result.

Evaluation combines numerical checks through Table-value Alignment with rubric-based semantic and visual judgments from a multimodal language model. The tested state-of-the-art models achieve below 50% overall performance. These results expose substantial gaps across the benchmark’s professional visualization workflows. By testing numerical accuracy, visual meaning, adaptation, and interaction together, DV-World provides a broader basis for assessing agents intended for enterprise visualization work.
icml-2026-dv-world-benchmarking-data-vis.tldr: DV-World tests visualization agents on 260 realistic creation, repair, adaptation, and interaction tasks, where evaluated models score below 50% overall.

paragraphs: Medical imaging models can perform unevenly across demographic groups. Combining models trained at different institutions could help by drawing on more diverse data, but differences between institutions can also produce conflicting updates. In one-shot federated learning, those conflicts must be handled within a single communication round.

Fair-FedMOE addresses the problem during both local training and aggregation. Locally, learnable prototypes route samples to group-specific experts, supporting specialized learning of subgroup features without inter-group interference. During aggregation, prototype similarities determine personalized weights, while differentiated aggregation strategies filter conflicting updates. The prototypes thus guide both where learning happens and how institutional contributions are combined.

The paper also introduces RES-AUC, a fairness measure inspired by Rawlsian justice that emphasizes worst-group performance and remains stable as the number of groups increases. Experiments using retinal and chest X-ray datasets with multiple foundation models report consistent fairness improvements without sacrificing accuracy. The findings support coordinating subgroup specialization and model aggregation to reduce disparities in the evaluated settings.
icml-2026-fair-fedmoe-group-fair-one-sho.tldr: Fair-FedMOE uses subgroup experts and prototype-guided aggregation to improve medical imaging fairness in one-shot federated learning without sacrificing reported accuracy.

paragraphs: Neural operators learn mappings between functions, making them useful as fast approximations to partial differential equation solvers. They commonly receive coordinates and function values as input. This paper asks whether supplying derivative information can reduce the work a network must do to learn the equation’s underlying differential structure.

Using Picard iteration on mild solutions, the authors show that input derivatives appear explicitly in the solution operator. They prove an improvement in approximation bounds from O(W^{-(s-m)/d}) to O(W^{-s/d}) when derivative features are supplied. Here, W is parameter count, s is input regularity, m is equation order, and d is spatial dimension.

Their analysis also finds that the optimal derivative order is strictly below the PDE’s order, reflecting a spectral bias–variance tradeoff. The proposed del-NO augmentation learns fractional derivative orders from data, providing automatic spectral regularization. Across the tested problems and architectures, it consistently improves prediction accuracy. The learned orders reflect physical structure while adjusting for noise and finite samples, explaining why directly matching the equation’s order need not be optimal.
icml-2026-fractional-is-better-learnable.tldr: Learnable fractional derivative features improve neural operator approximation and prediction while balancing physical structure against noise and finite-sample effects.

paragraphs: Prior-data fitted networks can estimate causal effects by treating a dataset as context for prediction. This paper asks whether their uncertainty estimates behave appropriately as more data becomes available. It focuses on the average treatment effect and its relationship to classical frequentist estimation.

The authors show that existing networks, interpreted as Bayesian estimators, can retain confounding bias induced by their prior. More data does not necessarily overwrite that influence, preventing frequentist consistency. They propose a one-step posterior correction to calibrate the estimates. Their theory shows that this correction helps restore consistency and can yield a semiparametric Bernstein–von Mises result, connecting calibrated posterior behavior to classical efficient estimators as data grows.

To implement the correction, the researchers construct martingale posteriors on top of the networks, recovering the functional nuisance posteriors that calibration requires. In multiple synthetic and semisynthetic experiments, the calibrated models produce treatment-effect uncertainty that asymptotically matches frequentist uncertainty and is well calibrated in finite samples compared with other Bayesian estimators.
icml-2026-frequentist-consistency-of-pri.tldr: A posterior correction helps causal prior-data fitted networks overcome persistent prior bias and produce uncertainty aligned with frequentist estimation.

paragraphs: Predicting kidney transplant survival requires combining functional biomarkers with patient characteristics while accounting for censoring. Censoring means that the survival outcome is not fully observed for every patient. FunCQNet addresses these issues through a neural network designed to predict multiple quantiles of survival, rather than compressing the prediction into a single value.

The method combines deep networks with a sequential quantile loss adjusted for censoring. It approximates coefficient functions that depend on interactions, allowing functional biomarker effects to vary with patient characteristics. The authors also introduce conformal inference to assess the significance of interactions between functional and scalar variables, connecting predictive modeling with interpretable statistical assessment.

Simulations show that the method robustly recovers functional effects across different noise and censoring levels. Applied to kidney transplant data, it produces precise predictions across multiple quantiles and identifies clinically significant, age-dependent interaction patterns involving donor type and recipient survival. These results demonstrate how the framework can describe variation in predicted survival while exposing interaction patterns relevant to interpreting its predictions.
icml-2026-funcqnet-a-functional-censored.tldr: FunCQNet models censored kidney transplant survival across multiple quantiles while assessing interactions between functional biomarkers and patient characteristics.

paragraphs: Mamba2 uses an expanded internal state to model temporal information, but that state creates substantial inference overhead during autoregressive generation. The paper identifies bandwidth saturation as a bottleneck. Removing scattered weights leaves activations dense, while weight magnitude alone misses runtime behavior and gradient-based selection is computationally costly.

GHOST performs structured pruning through an approximation to balanced truncation, a control-theoretic approach to reducing a system’s internal state. It jointly considers controllability and observability: how state components are affected and how they contribute to outputs. These measurements come entirely from forward-pass statistics, avoiding the need for backpropagation during selection.

The authors report fidelity comparable to gradient-based methods. Across models ranging from 130 million to 2.7 billion parameters, GHOST reduces the state dimension by 50% with an approximately one-point perplexity increase on WikiText-2. This result demonstrates a substantial state reduction with a measured language-modeling tradeoff. The approach targets the structure responsible for dense state overhead, while using runtime-sensitive information to decide what can be removed.
icml-2026-ghost-unmasking-phantom-states.tldr: GHOST uses forward-pass statistics to halve Mamba2 state dimensions with approximately one additional perplexity point on WikiText-2.

paragraphs: Combining language, sound, and visual information into one representation can cause a model to favor the easiest signal and overlook weaker but useful ones. It can also encourage reliance on incidental relationships between modalities. Group Cognition Learning addresses these problems through a governed collaboration process after each modality has been encoded separately.

The first stage controls information exchange. A Routing Agent proposes directed interactions, and an Auditing Agent assigns gates for each sample, emphasizing exchanges that add predictive value while suppressing redundant coupling. The second stage forms a consensus: a Public-Factor Agent maintains shared information, while an Aggregation Agent weights contributions to produce the final prediction.

Throughout this process, each modality retains a representation for its specialized information. Experiments on CMU-MOSI, CMU-MOSEI, and MIntRec report reduced modality dominance and spurious coupling, alongside state-of-the-art results on the evaluated regression and classification benchmarks. Additional analyses support the design. The findings suggest that controlling which modalities exchange information, and how their contributions are combined, can improve multimodal prediction.
icml-2026-group-cognition-learning-makin.tldr: Group Cognition Learning governs cross-modal exchanges and contribution weighting to reduce modality dominance and improve multimodal prediction.

paragraphs: Linear attention stores information in a fixed-size memory, whose updates depend on a state-transition or decay matrix. Rank-one approximations make these matrices cheaper to construct, but also restrict their expressive capacity. This paper investigates how to enrich the updates without introducing substantial extra cost.

Head-in-Head adds a mask matrix inside an individual attention head. Inspired by multi-head attention, the mask organizes partitions of the memory and controls interactions among them. This enables a rank-r approximation of the decay matrix using only a few additional parameters, while strengthening information exchange within a head. Mask normalization and chunk-wise parallelization support efficient parallel training.

Experiments on synthetic benchmarks and language modeling tasks consistently improve the evaluated baselines. Visual analyses connect those improvements to greater information diversity and stronger interactions inside individual heads. The contribution is therefore a change to how each head organizes and updates its memory, giving the model more expressive state transitions while retaining an efficient design suitable for parallel training.
icml-2026-head-in-head-in-linear-attenti.tldr: Head-in-Head adds structured interactions within linear-attention heads to make memory updates more expressive with few extra parameters.

paragraphs: Attribution methods explain predictions by assigning importance to parts of an input. For these explanations to be reliable, they should resist adversarial manipulation. Existing approaches often encourage that robustness with explicit regularization, which can be computationally expensive. This paper investigates whether ordinary training dynamics can provide robustness implicitly.

The authors connect curvature in parameter space with curvature in input space to theoretically motivate robustness arising through stochastic gradient descent. They validate the effect across architectures, datasets, and attribution methods, reporting negligible computational overhead. This makes learning dynamics themselves a practical mechanism for improving the stability of explanations.

The paper also identifies a specific boundary: these robustness gains often fail to transfer to attention-based attribution when attention uses softmax normalization. The authors link this failure to inherent entropy constraints, proving and experimentally validating the limitation. Replacing softmax with kernel-based attention restores the gains in the studied transformer models. The results therefore connect robust attribution to both training dynamics and the normalization used by the explanation mechanism.
icml-2026-improving-adversarial-robustne.tldr: Standard training dynamics can improve attribution robustness, while kernel-based attention addresses a softmax-related barrier to those gains in transformers.

paragraphs: Chaotic systems are sensitive to initial conditions, making exact long-term forecasts infeasible, especially with noisy observations. A useful learned emulator can instead aim to reproduce the system’s long-term statistical behavior. Existing approaches to that goal often depend on manually chosen summary statistics or large datasets covering multiple environments.

This paper proposes adversarial optimal transport objectives that jointly learn useful summary statistics and a physically consistent emulator from a single noisy trajectory. The learning objective therefore helps determine which statistical features matter while also training the simulated dynamics. The authors study two versions: a Sinkhorn divergence formulation associated with 2-Wasserstein transport and a WGAN-style dual formulation associated with 1-Wasserstein transport.

Both formulations receive theoretical analysis and experimental validation. Numerical experiments span several chaotic systems, including high-dimensional systems with chaos evolving across space and time. The proposed objectives significantly improve long-term statistical fidelity. That result concerns how well the learned dynamics reproduce aggregate behavior over time; the paper’s stated forecasting challenge remains the sensitivity that makes exact long-term trajectories infeasible.
icml-2026-learning-to-emulate-chaos-adve.tldr: Adversarial optimal transport objectives learn chaotic emulators from a single noisy trajectory and improve their long-term statistical fidelity.

paragraphs: Difficult reasoning problems can deny language models a useful training signal when neither the model nor a stronger model can generate a correct solution. Human expert solutions offer another source of supervision, but they often leave steps implicit for human readers. Direct imitation can consequently struggle with a mismatch between expert presentation and model reasoning.

Distribution Aligned Imitation Learning addresses that mismatch through two-step self-distillation. First, it transforms expert solutions into detailed reasoning traces aligned with the model’s distribution. Second, a contrastive objective focuses training on the insights and methods contributed by the expert. This separates making a solution learnable from emphasizing the knowledge that makes it valuable.

Using fewer than 1,000 high-quality expert solutions, the authors report up to 31% gains in pass@128 on Qwen2.5-Instruct and Qwen3, doubled reasoning efficiency, and generalization beyond the training domain. The results support adapting the form of expert demonstrations before learning from them, particularly when expensive expert examples must provide training signals that transfer across problems.
icml-2026-making-expert-reasoning-learna.tldr: DAIL converts expert solutions into model-aligned reasoning traces, enabling sample-efficient reasoning improvements from fewer than 1,000 expert examples.

paragraphs: Mechanistic interpretability seeks subnetworks, often called circuits, that explain a model’s behavior. This paper argues that discovering a circuit should be treated as statistical estimation. A circuit’s scientific usefulness depends partly on whether it remains stable when the data or analysis choices change.

The authors trace instability to causal mediation analysis, which underlies component-effect measurements. Even exact scores for individual inputs have high intrinsic variance, meaning that a component’s measured causal effect varies substantially with the input. Circuit discovery then inherits this variation. Fast approximations such as Edge Attribution Patching add estimation noise, and aggregation across a dataset can produce fragile structural estimates.

The analysis shows that small changes to inputs or hyperparameters can yield very different circuits. By decomposing the sources of variance, the paper explains how uncertainty at the level of individual causal scores can propagate into uncertainty about an entire subnetwork. It advocates routine stability reporting and stronger statistical robustness practices so that circuit findings can be assessed as estimates with variability.
icml-2026-mechanistic-interpretability-a.tldr: Circuit discovery inherits and amplifies variable causal-effect estimates, motivating routine statistical stability checks in mechanistic interpretability.

paragraphs: Single-cell perturbation models aim to predict how gene expression changes after an intervention. Yet recent benchmarks often rank them below simply predicting the dataset mean. Through large-scale simulations and analysis of two real datasets, this paper traces that surprising outcome to how prediction error is measured when perturbation effects are sparse.

Unweighted metrics systematically reward mean predictions because the relatively few affected genes contribute only a small part of the overall score. The authors introduce metrics aware of differentially expressed genes: weighted mean-squared error and weighted delta R-squared. These metrics emphasize perturbation-specific signals. Explicit negative and positive performance baselines provide reference points for interpreting the resulting scores.

Under this framework, predicting the mean receives null performance, while informative predictions receive appropriate credit. The authors also use weighted mean-squared error as a training objective, reducing mode collapse and improving performance across multiple model architectures. The findings connect evaluation and learning: emphasizing the sparse response signal changes both which models appear useful and which predictions training encourages.
icml-2026-needles-in-the-haystack-addres.tldr: Gene-aware weighting corrects metrics that favor mean predictions and improves training for sparse single-cell perturbation responses.

paragraphs: Linear attention reduces the computational growth associated with softmax attention, but can lose expressive information. This paper identifies two mechanisms: normalization removes the query’s magnitude, weakening its connection to how concentrated attention becomes, and common non-negativity transformations discard valid inner-product interactions.

NaLaFormer separates query and key vectors into magnitude and direction. It inserts query magnitude into the attention kernel so that the attention distribution can again respond to that quantity. Direction is handled through a geometric cosine-based similarity that guarantees non-negative values while preserving fine-grained inner-product information. Each component of the decomposition therefore addresses a different source of lost expressiveness.

The evaluations report gains of up to 7.5% in ImageNet-1K accuracy and 4.7% in ADE20K mIoU over comparable baselines. In super-resolution tasks with more than 70,000 tokens, peak memory falls by 92.3%. The model also exceeds strong baselines such as Mamba on common-sense reasoning and achieves state-of-the-art Long Range Arena results. Together, these findings support the decomposition across the tested visual and sequence-processing tasks.
icml-2026-norm-times-direction-restoring.tldr: NaLaFormer restores query magnitude and preserves directional interactions to improve linear attention’s accuracy and efficiency across evaluated tasks.

paragraphs: Video reasoning becomes easier to inspect when a model identifies where and when its supporting evidence appears. Open-o3-Video addresses this by incorporating timestamps, objects, and bounding boxes into reasoning traces. Its non-agent framework connects answers to explicit evidence across changing scenes.

The researchers construct STGR datasets that provide unified spatial and temporal supervision. They then use a cold-start reinforcement learning strategy whose rewards jointly encourage accurate answers, temporal alignment, and spatial precision. This training design treats locating relevant evidence as part of the reasoning task, alongside producing the answer itself.

On V-STAR, the model achieves state-of-the-art performance, with reported improvements of 14.4% in mAM and 24.2% in mLGM over Qwen2.5-VL. It also shows consistent gains across other video understanding benchmarks. The grounded traces support confidence-aware test-time scaling, which improves answer reliability. These findings link explicit evidence localization to both stronger benchmark results and a reasoning process whose cited moments and regions can be checked against the video.
icml-2026-open-o3-video-grounded-video-r.tldr: Open-o3-Video grounds reasoning in timestamps and bounding boxes, improving video understanding and supporting more reliable answers.

paragraphs: Brain-network prediction models often learn connectivity representations first and add phenotype information only near the final classifier. PhenoBrain challenges the assumption behind that separation: the same functional connectivity pattern may support different conclusions under different phenotype contexts. It therefore lets phenotype information shape how the network representation is learned.

The framework introduces phenotype-conditioned routing for long-range communication. A subject-specific multi-hop communication kernel models interactions across the connectome, allowing phenotype context to influence how information travels through the brain network. A second mechanism uses phenotypic information as a conditional prior to regulate attention learning. Both components affect the model’s internal processing before the final prediction.

The authors construct two multimodal brain-network analysis datasets from open-source imaging data and report state-of-the-art performance in extensive experiments. The findings support conditioning connectivity analysis on phenotype context in the evaluated prediction settings. The methodological contribution is the placement of that context within routing and attention, so it influences which network relationships the model develops and emphasizes.
icml-2026-phenobrain-phenotype-condition.tldr: PhenoBrain uses phenotype context to shape long-range communication and attention within brain-network models, improving performance on two constructed datasets.

paragraphs: Music recordings can contain several quality problems at once, including distortion, excessive reverberation, clipping, tonal imbalance, and reduced stereo width. Correcting them typically involves separate tools and manual adjustments. SonicMaster brings restoration and mastering into one generative model that accepts natural-language instructions or operates automatically for general restoration.

The researchers create paired degraded and high-quality tracks by applying nineteen simulated degradation functions. These cover five enhancement groups: equalization, dynamics, reverb, amplitude, and stereo. The model trains through flow matching to transform degraded audio into cleaned and mastered output, with text prompts guiding the requested enhancement.

Objective audio-quality measurements show significant improvements across all artifact categories, and subjective listening tests find that listeners prefer SonicMaster’s outputs over the evaluated baselines. These two forms of evaluation support both measurable improvement and listener preference. The approach matters because one model can address a broad range of recording problems while allowing the user to specify a targeted change or request general restoration.
icml-2026-sonicmaster-towards-controllab.tldr: SonicMaster unifies music restoration and mastering with text-guided or automatic enhancement, improving measured quality and listener preference.

paragraphs: Vision-language models need image and text representations that occupy a compatible semantic space. Building that alignment can require substantial paired data, even when pretrained encoders are connected through lightweight mappings. This paper explores a source of semantic information already present in supervised vision models: the weights of their classification heads.

The authors repurpose these weights as semantic prototypes instead of discarding them after pretraining. The prototypes serve two roles. They can act as semantic anchors for zero-shot alignment, and they can augment training data by being mixed with real image-text pairs. Both uses draw additional value from the classification knowledge stored in the pretrained model.

The method integrates with several state-of-the-art post-hoc alignment techniques and consistently improves accuracy on cross-modal retrieval and zero- and few-shot classification tasks. These results show that a component commonly removed after supervised pretraining can remain useful when connecting visual and language representations. The contribution is a reusable source of semantic structure that supports alignment directly and strengthens learning from available paired examples.
icml-2026-supervised-classification-head.tldr: Recycling pretrained classification weights as semantic prototypes improves vision-language alignment through zero-shot anchoring and data augmentation.

paragraphs: Agent trajectory datasets record sequences of problem-solving behavior and can be costly to produce. ActHook introduces a watermarking method for these datasets, aiming to make their use detectable through the behavior of a trained agent. The method draws inspiration from software hooks inserted at particular execution points.

ActHook adds hook actions that activate in response to a secret input key while preserving the original task outcome. Because an agent acts sequentially, these actions can be placed at decision points without disrupting task flow. An agent trained on the marked trajectories can then produce the hook actions at a substantially higher rate when the activation key appears.

That behavioral signal supports black-box detection, using observable agent behavior. Experiments cover mathematical reasoning, web search, and software engineering agents. On Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B, the method achieves an average detection AUC of 94.3 with negligible performance degradation. The reported result supports tracing dataset use through learned, selectively activated actions while maintaining task performance in the evaluated settings.
icml-2026-watermarking-llm-agent-traject.tldr: ActHook embeds secret-key-triggered actions in agent trajectories to enable black-box detection of dataset use with negligible reported performance degradation.

paragraphs: Identifying a text’s language helps organize multilingual datasets and evaluate language models. Although existing systems perform very well on widely represented languages, they can struggle with scarce training data and closely related languages. UniLID approaches this problem through the probabilistic machinery of UnigramLM tokenization.

For a given string, the method compares how likely it is under each language’s unigram distribution and predicts the most likely language. It uses the tokenizer’s parameter estimation and inference methods to make this approach efficient. New languages can be added incrementally without retraining existing models, and the method can fit naturally into language-model tokenization pipelines.

Evaluations against fastText, GlotLID-M, and CLD3 show competitive results on standard benchmarks, substantially better sample efficiency in low-resource settings, and large gains in fine-grained dialect identification. In the reported low-resource evaluations, UniLID surpasses 70% accuracy with as few as five labeled samples per language. These findings highlight how a tokenizer’s probability model can also provide a practical signal for language identification.
icml-2026-what-language-is-this-ask-your.tldr: UniLID identifies languages using tokenizer probabilities, improving low-resource sample efficiency and fine-grained dialect recognition.

paragraphs: WhisperSplat hides a full-resolution two-dimensional image in a single view of a 3D Gaussian Splatting model while preserving rendering quality elsewhere. Earlier approaches embed data by retraining or changing model weights, which can affect novel views and restrict capacity. This method instead learns a small noise key specific to the selected view.

The key is applied to each Gaussian’s spherical-harmonic features, allowing the hidden image to be recovered through rendering with the key. Other views remain indistinguishable from the original renders. Training uses Gradual Pixel Perturbation with a cosine-decay schedule, first encouraging rapid departure from the clean image and then shifting to a combined reconstruction and structural-similarity objective.

An optional lightweight refiner can further improve recovered image quality, without requiring the large pretrained decoders used by some prior approaches. Across nine standard scenes, WhisperSplat reports better hidden-image recovery than methods including GS-Hider and KeySS while preserving clean model performance. The lossless claim concerns preserving the original rendering quality; recovery quality is separately evaluated and can benefit from refinement.
icml-2026-whispersplat-lossless-steganog.tldr: WhisperSplat uses a view-specific noise key to hide an image in a 3D Gaussian Splatting scene while preserving clean rendering quality.
